# Torn Tire Tread and Sidewall on Subaru Impreza

A curb strike can turn a routine commute into an urgent mechanical puzzle. In the case of a 2012 Subaru Impreza, hitting that edge likely caused the specific damage you are seeing: a tear in the tread and a separate compromise to the sidewall. While the immediate instinct is to question whether replacing all four tires on an all-wheel-drive (AWD) system is mandatory, the reality depends entirely on the extent of the structural damage, not just the drivetrain configuration.

The presence of a sidewall tear immediately shifts the decision from "should I replace two?" to "the tire must be replaced." Sidewall rubber is under constant flexion during normal driving; once the integrity of that vertical wall is breached, the internal steel belts are exposed. This is not merely a surface scratch. If you drive on a compromised sidewall, the heat generated by friction and flexing can melt the internal structure, leading to a sudden blowout at highway speeds. There is no patch or sealant solution for a puncture in the sidewall zone that meets safety standards. The tire is functionally dead regardless of tread depth.

Regarding the transmission concern often cited with AWD vehicles: it stems from the need to maintain equal rotational diameter between all four wheels. If you mount one new tire alongside three old ones, the new tire will be slightly larger in circumference. As the car moves, the drivetrain must constantly slip gears or engage the viscous coupler/differential clutch packs to compensate for this discrepancy. Over a short distance like a tow trip, modern AWD systems can handle this. However, sustained driving on mismatched tires puts unnecessary stress on the center differential and transfer case. It is not an immediate death sentence if you are careful, but it is an avoidable source of wear that increases repair costs later.

You mentioned performing the penny test on the remaining three tires. If those tires also show significant wear or low tread depth relative to the new one, replacing all four becomes a logical economic decision rather than a forced safety mandate. When purchasing new tires for a 2012 model year vehicle, consider that you are likely approaching the end of the tire life cycle for the remaining set anyway. The cost of labor to mount and balance four tires is often similar to two, making the price difference per tire negligible in the grand scheme.

If you decide to proceed with replacing only the damaged pair, ensure the new tires are matched as closely as possible to the original equipment specifications. For a 2012 Impreza, this usually means maintaining the factory size and load index. While staggered setups exist for performance builds, most daily drivers require uniform tire dimensions to keep the AWD system happy.

Before you head to the shop, verify your current tire pressure against the door jamb sticker. Low pressure exacerbates sidewall damage during impact. If the remaining tires are already at their wear limit, as your penny test suggests, swapping them now ensures you don't face a scenario where you must replace all four immediately after the initial repair, doubling your labor costs in six months.

For those managing vehicle maintenance logs or fleet records, documenting the curb strike and the specific nature of the failure (sidewall vs. tread) is crucial for warranty claims if applicable, though tires under one year old typically fall under manufacturer defect policies only if they fail prematurely due to manufacturing flaws, not impact damage. Always prioritize structural integrity over cost savings when dealing with AWD systems; a small extra expense now prevents catastrophic drivetrain stress later.
